questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a General Polynomial
questions.worked_solution:
We identify the leading term and compute its limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }({x}^{5}+4) & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }({x}^{5}) \\  & =-\infty \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Root of a Transformed Exponential Function
questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
5(7)^{x}-35=0
$$

First, we isolate the term with the variable exponent by adding $35$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}5(7)^{x}-35 & =0 \\ 5(7)^{x}-\cancel{35}+\cancel{35} & =0+35 \\ 5(7)^{x} & =35\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing both sides by $5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5(7)^{x} & =35 \\ {7}^{x} & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(7)$, we equate the exponents. This gives

$$
x=1.
$$

Therefore, the root of $f(x)$ is $x=1.$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Root of a Transformed Exponential Function

What is the total surface area of the cube above if it is $4\,\text{cm}$ long, $4\,\text{cm}$ wide, and $4\,\text{cm}$ tall?

$$

$$

From the diagram, we have squares only.

The squares are $4\,\text{cm}$ long and $4\,\text{cm}$ high. So, the area of one square is:

$$
\text{Area of the square}=4\times 4=16\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the cube consists of $6$ squares.

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Cotangent Function
questions.problem: If $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=7$ for some $x$, then find the value of $\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+12\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
The period of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ is $\pi .$ Therefore, for integer $n$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=12$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+12\cdot \pi )=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+12\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=7,$ then $\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+12\pi )=7.$

provenance.kp_title: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Cotangent Function

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Exponential Equation by Factoring
questions.problem: What is the product of solutions of the equation ${x}^{2}\cdot {4}^{3x}-25\cdot {4}^{3x}=0?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot {4}^{3x}-25\cdot {4}^{3x} & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-25)\cdot {4}^{3x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
{x}^{2}-25=0\,\text{and}\,{4}^{3x}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation ${x}^{2}-25=0$ can be factored as

$$
(x+5)(x-5)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-5,5.$

- The equation ${4}^{3x}=0$ has no solutions because ${4}^{3x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, the original equation has the solutions $x=-5,5,$ and their product is $(-5)\cdot 5=-25.$

provenance.kp_title: Solving an Exponential Equation by Factoring

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Roots of a Transformed Radical Function With an Odd Index
questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
\sqrt[7]{3x+13}-1=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[7]{3x+13}-1 & =0 \\ \sqrt[7]{3x+13} & =1 \\ (\sqrt[7]{3x+13})^{7} & ={1}^{7} \\ 3x+13 & =1 \\ 3x & =-12 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the root of $f(x)$ is $x=-4.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Roots of a Transformed Radical Function With an Odd Index

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules
questions.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=(x+1)^{2}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x+3.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2(x+1),\,{v}^{′}(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)\cdot (x+3)-(x+1)^{2}\cdot 1}{(x+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)[2(x+3)-(x+1)]}{{(x+3)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)[2x+6-x-1]}{{(x+3)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)(x+5)}{{(x+3)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Equation of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point
questions.problem:
Find the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{8}{{x}^{2}}$ at the point $(2,2).$

$x\,-$
{{field-1}}$\cdot \,y\,=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{8}{{x}^{2}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{8}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{x}^{-2}) \\  & =-16{x}^{-3} \\  & =-\frac{16}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,2):$

$$
m={f}^{′}(2)=-\frac{16}{(2)^{3}}=-\frac{16}{8}=-2
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{-2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(2) & =\frac{1}{2}(x-2) \\ 2y-4 & =x-2 \\ x-2\cdot y & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Determining the Equation of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Sums and Scalar Multiplication of Vectors
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
b=i-j-k=⟨1,-1,-1⟩.
$$

To compute $a-2b,$ we just need to perform the required operations with each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}a-2b & =⟨0,0,0⟩-2\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0,0⟩-⟨2\cdot 1,2\cdot (-1),2\cdot (-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0,0⟩-⟨2,-2,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,2,2⟩ \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
